description: Comprehensive question bank for Food Science and Nutrition (FDA & SDA competitive examination). Questions derived from the provided Food Science and Nutrition study material covering Food Science, Nutrition and Public Health, food preservation and safety, nutrients and deficiency disorders, maternal and child nutrition, food security, ICDS/Anganwadi Services, PM POSHAN and POSHAN Abhiyaan/POSHAN 2.0. Verify current programme details from official sources before formal examination use.

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food science?

options.A: The study of only cooking methods
options.B: The study of the physical, chemical, biological and technological properties of food

questions.explanation: Food science is the study of the physical, chemical, biological and technological properties of food, including its composition, processing, preservation, safety, quality and storage.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food?

options.A: Any edible substance consumed only for taste
options.B: Any safe, edible substance consumed to provide energy, nutrients and other components needed for growth, maintenance, repair and health

questions.explanation: Food is any safe, edible substance consumed to provide energy, nutrients and other components needed for growth, maintenance, repair and health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food composition?

options.A: The colour of food
options.B: The amounts of water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and other substances present in a food

questions.explanation: Food composition refers to the amounts of water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and other substances present in a food.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Which of the following are major components of food?

options.A: Water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre

questions.explanation: Water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre are major components; foods also contain pigments, flavour compounds and other bioactive substances.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is nutritional value?

options.A: The price of a food
options.B: The nutrients and energy a food provides relative to the amount consumed

questions.explanation: Nutritional value describes the nutrients and energy a food provides relative to the amount consumed.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Which of the following are examples of basic food groups?

options.A: Cereals and millets; pulses and legumes; milk and animal-source foods; vegetables; fruits; nuts and oilseeds; fats and oils

questions.explanation: Common groupings include cereals and millets; pulses and legumes; milk and animal-source foods; vegetables; fruits; nuts and oilseeds; and fats and oils. Grouping systems vary by dietary guide.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Why is dietary diversity important?

options.A: Different foods provide different nutrients, reducing the risk of nutrient gaps and supporting dietary adequacy

questions.explanation: Different foods provide different nutrients. A diverse diet helps reduce the risk of nutrient gaps and supports overall dietary adequacy.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food processing?

options.A: Only cooking food
options.B: Operations that transform raw ingredients into edible products or improve safety, shelf life, convenience, quality or digestibility

questions.explanation: Food processing includes operations that transform raw ingredients into edible products or improve safety, shelf life, convenience, quality or digestibility.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food preservation?

options.A: Using physical, chemical or biological methods to slow or prevent spoilage and maintain food safety and quality

questions.explanation: Food preservation uses physical, chemical or biological methods to slow or prevent spoilage and maintain food safety and quality.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What causes food spoilage?

options.A: Only microorganisms
options.B: Microorganisms, enzymes, oxidation, moisture changes, pests, physical damage or unsuitable storage conditions

questions.explanation: Spoilage may result from microorganisms, enzymes, oxidation, moisture changes, pests, physical damage or unsuitable storage conditions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Which of the following are common signs of food spoilage?

options.A: Unusual odour, colour or texture, mould growth, gas formation, slime, package swelling or abnormal taste

questions.explanation: Unusual odour, colour or texture, mould growth, gas formation, slime, package swelling or abnormal taste may indicate spoilage. Do not taste food to test safety.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is refrigeration?

options.A: Storage at low but generally non-freezing temperatures that slows microbial growth and chemical reactions
options.B: Freezing food at very low temperatures

questions.explanation: Storage at low but generally non-freezing temperatures slows microbial growth and chemical reactions; it does not sterilise food or stop all spoilage.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Does refrigeration kill all disease-causing microorganisms?

options.A: Yes, it kills all microorganisms
options.B: No, it only slows the growth of many microorganisms; some can survive and certain organisms can grow slowly at refrigerator temperatures

questions.explanation: Refrigeration slows the growth of many microorganisms, but some can survive and certain organisms can grow slowly at refrigerator temperatures.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is freezing?

options.A: Converting much of the food's water into ice, greatly slowing microbial growth and many deterioration reactions

questions.explanation: Freezing converts much of the food's water into ice and greatly slows microbial growth and many deterioration reactions; it does not reliably kill all microorganisms.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Can thawed food be refrozen?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: It depends on how it was thawed and kept; food thawed safely under refrigeration may generally be refrozen, though quality can decline; food held at unsafe temperatures should not be refrozen as a way to make it safe

questions.explanation: It depends on how it was thawed and kept. Food thawed safely under refrigeration may generally be refrozen, though quality can decline; food held at unsafe temperatures should not be refrozen as a way to make it safe.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is drying or dehydration?

options.A: Removal of water from food to lower water activity and inhibit microbial growth

questions.explanation: Removal of water from food lowers water activity and inhibits microbial growth; methods include sun drying, hot-air drying, spray drying and freeze-drying.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is water activity (aw)?

options.A: The total moisture content of food
options.B: A measure of the availability of water for microbial growth and chemical reactions; it is not the same as total moisture content
options.C: The amount of water added during processing
options.D: The amount of water lost during drying

questions.explanation: Water activity (aw) measures the availability of water for microbial growth and chemical reactions; it is not the same as total moisture content.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is pasteurisation?

options.A: A controlled heat treatment designed to destroy specified pathogenic microorganisms and reduce spoilage organisms in a food, followed by appropriate storage
options.B: Freezing food to very low temperatures

questions.explanation: Pasteurisation is a controlled heat treatment designed to destroy specified pathogenic microorganisms and reduce spoilage organisms in a food, followed by appropriate storage.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Does pasteurisation make milk sterile?

options.A: Yes, it makes milk sterile
options.B: No, pasteurisation reduces pathogens to an accepted level but does not make milk sterile; it must still be handled and stored correctly

questions.explanation: Pasteurisation reduces pathogens to an accepted level but does not make milk sterile; it must still be handled and stored correctly.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is UHT processing?

options.A: Ultra-high-temperature processing that heats a product to a high temperature for a short time and aseptically packages it, allowing extended shelf life when unopened

questions.explanation: Ultra-high-temperature processing heats a product to a high temperature for a short time and aseptically packages it, allowing extended shelf life when unopened.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is canning?

options.A: A preservation method in which food is sealed in a container and heat-processed to destroy relevant microorganisms and enzymes
options.D: A method of adding preservatives to food

questions.explanation: Canning is a preservation method in which food is sealed in a container and heat-processed to destroy relevant microorganisms and enzymes; low-acid foods require carefully validated processing to control Clostridium botulinum.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is fermentation?

options.A: A process in which microorganisms or their enzymes convert food components, often sugars, into acids, gases or alcohol, changing flavour, texture and shelf life
options.D: A process of adding chemicals to food

questions.explanation: Fermentation is a process in which microorganisms or their enzymes convert food components, often sugars, into acids, gases or alcohol, changing flavour, texture and shelf life.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: Which of the following are examples of fermented foods?

options.A: Curd/yoghurt, idli and dosa batter, some pickles, fermented vegetables, bread and certain traditional beverages

questions.explanation: Curd/yoghurt, idli and dosa batter, some pickles, fermented vegetables, bread and certain traditional beverages are examples of fermented foods.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is food packaging?

options.A: Packaging contains and protects food during handling, storage and transport and can provide information, tamper evidence and barriers to moisture, oxygen, light or contamination

questions.explanation: Packaging contains and protects food during handling, storage and transport and can provide information, tamper evidence and barriers to moisture, oxygen, light or contamination.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of food packaging?

options.A: Containment, protection, preservation, convenience, communication and traceability

questions.explanation: The main functions of food packaging are containment, protection, preservation, convenience, communication and traceability.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What is modified-atmosphere packaging?

options.A: A packaging method in which the gas composition around food is changed to slow selected deterioration processes

questions.explanation: Modified-atmosphere packaging is a packaging method in which the gas composition around food is changed to slow selected deterioration processes; it must be designed for the particular food and cold chain.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food contamination?

options.A: The presence or introduction of biological, chemical or physical hazards into food, making it unsafe or unsuitable
options.B: The addition of nutrients to food

questions.explanation: Food contamination is the presence or introduction of biological, chemical or physical hazards into food, making it unsafe or unsuitable.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are biological food hazards?

options.A: Bacteria, viruses, parasites, moulds and their toxins

questions.explanation: Bacteria, viruses, parasites, moulds and their toxins are biological hazards.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Which of the following are examples of chemical food hazards?

options.A: Pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, cleaning chemicals, heavy metals, naturally occurring toxins and excessive or unauthorised additives

questions.explanation: Examples include pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, cleaning chemicals, heavy metals, naturally occurring toxins and excessive or unauthorised additives.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are physical food hazards?

options.A: Foreign objects such as glass, metal fragments, stones, hard plastic, wood or other materials that may cause injury

questions.explanation: Physical food hazards are foreign objects such as glass, metal fragments, stones, hard plastic, wood or other materials that may cause injury.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is cross-contamination?

options.A: Transfer of harmful microorganisms or allergens from one food, surface, utensil or person to another
options.D: The process of adding nutrients to food

questions.explanation: Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful microorganisms or allergens from one food, surface, utensil or person to another, for example from raw meat to ready-to-eat food.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food adulteration?

options.A: The intentional or sometimes accidental lowering of food quality or safety by substitution, removal or addition of an inferior, harmful or undeclared substance
options.B: The addition of vitamins to food

questions.explanation: Food adulteration is the intentional or sometimes accidental lowering of food quality or safety by substitution, removal or addition of an inferior, harmful or undeclared substance.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Which of the following are examples of food adulteration?

options.A: Dilution of milk with water, addition of non-permitted colours to spices, substitution of edible oils, or mixing foreign matter with grains

questions.explanation: Examples may include dilution of milk with water, addition of non-permitted colours to spices, substitution of edible oils, or mixing foreign matter with grains. Specific tests and legal findings must be based on validated methods.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are food additives?

options.A: Substances intentionally added to food for technological purposes such as preserving, colouring, sweetening, stabilising, emulsifying or regulating acidity, subject to food regulations

questions.explanation: Food additives are substances intentionally added to food for technological purposes such as preserving, colouring, sweetening, stabilising, emulsifying or regulating acidity, subject to food regulations.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is the difference between an additive and a contaminant?

options.A: An additive is intentionally used for a permitted technological purpose and must comply with standards; a contaminant enters food unintentionally or is present as an unwanted substance
options.C: An additive is always harmful; a contaminant is always safe
options.D: A contaminant is intentionally added; an additive is unintentional

questions.explanation: An additive is intentionally used for a permitted technological purpose and must comply with standards; a contaminant enters food unintentionally or is present as an unwanted substance.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are food preservatives?

options.A: Substances or methods used to slow microbial spoilage or other deterioration
options.B: Substances that add colour to food
options.C: Substances that add flavour to food
options.D: Substances that add nutrients to food

questions.explanation: Food preservatives are substances or methods used to slow microbial spoilage or other deterioration; examples of permitted preservative classes include benzoates and sorbates in specified foods and limits.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Are all preservatives harmful?

options.A: No, approved preservatives have specified permitted uses and limits; risk depends on substance, dose, food category and exposure; unauthorised use or excessive levels are unsafe
options.D: No, preservatives are always safe in any amount

questions.explanation: No. Approved preservatives have specified permitted uses and limits. Risk depends on substance, dose, food category and exposure; unauthorised use or excessive levels are unsafe.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food safety?

options.A: Assurance that food will not cause harm when prepared and/or eaten according to its intended use

questions.explanation: Food safety is the assurance that food will not cause harm when prepared and/or eaten according to its intended use.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food hygiene?

options.A: Conditions and practices that prevent contamination and keep food safe throughout production, preparation, storage, transport and service

questions.explanation: Food hygiene refers to conditions and practices that prevent contamination and keep food safe throughout production, preparation, storage, transport and service.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are the basic rules of food hygiene?

options.A: Keep clean; separate raw and cooked foods; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials

questions.explanation: The basic rules of food hygiene are: keep clean; separate raw and cooked foods; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is the food danger zone?

options.A: A commonly used food-safety teaching range of approximately 5°C to 60°C, in which many foodborne bacteria can multiply rapidly

questions.explanation: A commonly used food-safety teaching range is approximately 5°C to 60°C, in which many foodborne bacteria can multiply rapidly; exact regulatory limits and time controls may vary by food and jurisdiction.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What are foodborne diseases?

options.A: Illnesses caused by consuming food or water contaminated with pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, chemicals or parasites
options.B: Illnesses caused by eating too much food
options.C: Illnesses caused by food allergies only
options.D: Illnesses caused by nutritional deficiencies only

questions.explanation: Foodborne diseases are illnesses caused by consuming food or water contaminated with pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, chemicals or parasites.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Which of the following are important examples of foodborne pathogens?

options.A: Salmonella, pathogenic Escherichia coli, Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, norovirus and toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus

questions.explanation: Salmonella, pathogenic Escherichia coli, Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, norovirus and toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus are important examples of foodborne pathogens.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is botulism?

options.A: A potentially life-threatening illness caused by botulinum neurotoxin, commonly associated with improperly processed or stored foods
options.D: A type of food poisoning caused by pesticides

questions.explanation: Botulism is a potentially life-threatening illness caused by botulinum neurotoxin, commonly associated with improperly processed or stored foods; safe validated canning practices are essential.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is aflatoxin?

options.A: A group of toxic compounds produced by certain Aspergillus moulds, which can contaminate crops such as groundnuts and maize

questions.explanation: Aflatoxins are a group of toxic compounds produced by certain Aspergillus moulds, which can contaminate crops such as groundnuts and maize under favourable conditions; aflatoxins can damage the liver and some are carcinogenic.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food testing?

options.A: Analysis of food samples to assess identity, composition, quality, contaminants, residues, additives, microbiological safety and compliance with standards
options.B: Tasting food to check its flavour

questions.explanation: Food testing is the analysis of food samples to assess identity, composition, quality, contaminants, residues, additives, microbiological safety and compliance with standards.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What information does a food label provide?

options.A: Product identity, ingredients, allergens, nutrition information, net quantity, batch details, date marking, storage instructions and manufacturer or importer details

questions.explanation: A label provides prescribed information such as product identity, ingredients, allergens, nutrition information, net quantity, batch details, date marking, storage instructions and manufacturer or importer details.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is the role of FSSAI?

options.A: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India is the statutory authority established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, responsible for laying down science-based food standards and regulating food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import to ensure safe and wholesome food

questions.explanation: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India is the statutory authority established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, responsible for laying down science-based food standards and regulating food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import to ensure safe and wholesome food.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is HACCP?

options.A: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points — a preventive system that identifies food-safety hazards and establishes controls at critical points in a process
options.B: A type of food preservation method

questions.explanation: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points is a preventive system that identifies food-safety hazards and establishes controls at critical points in a process.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is food traceability?

options.A: The ability to track food and its ingredients through stages of production, processing and distribution

questions.explanation: Food traceability is the ability to track food and its ingredients through stages of production, processing and distribution.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is nutrition?

options.A: The process by which the body obtains and uses food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, regulation and maintenance of health

questions.explanation: Nutrition is the process by which the body obtains and uses food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, regulation and maintenance of health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are nutrients?

options.A: Substances in food required by the body, including carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water

questions.explanation: Nutrients are substances in food required by the body, including carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are macronutrients?

options.A: Nutrients required in relatively large amounts, principally carbohydrates, proteins and fats

questions.explanation: Macronutrients are nutrients required in relatively large amounts, principally carbohydrates, proteins and fats; water is also required in large amounts but does not provide energy.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are micronutrients?

options.A: Vitamins and minerals required in small amounts for normal growth, metabolism, immunity and other body functions

questions.explanation: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals required in small amounts for normal growth, metabolism, immunity and other body functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is a balanced diet?

options.A: A diet that supplies adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts and proportions for a person's age, sex, activity, physiological state and health
options.B: A diet that contains only fruits and vegetables
options.C: A diet that contains only cereals
options.D: A diet that contains only proteins

questions.explanation: A balanced diet supplies adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts and proportions for a person's age, sex, activity, physiological state and health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Does one balanced diet suit everyone?

options.A: No, requirements vary with age, sex, body size, physical activity, pregnancy, lactation, health status and other factors
options.C: Yes, a balanced diet is the same for all ages
options.D: No, only children need a balanced diet

questions.explanation: No. Requirements vary with age, sex, body size, physical activity, pregnancy, lactation, health status and other factors.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are the main functions of carbohydrates?

options.A: They are a major energy source; dietary fibre also supports bowel function and influences metabolic health
options.C: They are needed only for bone formation
options.D: They are needed only for blood clotting

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are a major energy source; dietary fibre also supports bowel function and influences metabolic health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of carbohydrates?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram for digestible carbohydrate

questions.explanation: The energy value of carbohydrates is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram for digestible carbohydrate, as a standard nutrition calculation factor.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are proteins?

options.A: Molecules made of amino acids needed for growth, tissue repair, enzymes, hormones, transport proteins and immune functions
options.B: Molecules made of fatty acids only

questions.explanation: Proteins are molecules made of amino acids and are needed for growth, tissue repair, enzymes, hormones, transport proteins and immune functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of protein?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of protein is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are essential amino acids?

options.A: Amino acids that the human body cannot synthesise in sufficient amounts and therefore must obtain from the diet
options.B: Amino acids that the body can synthesise in sufficient amounts
options.C: Amino acids found only in plant foods
options.D: Amino acids found only in animal foods

questions.explanation: Essential amino acids are amino acids that the human body cannot synthesise in sufficient amounts and therefore must obtain from the diet.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are fats?

options.A: Dietary fats provide concentrated energy, supply essential fatty acids, help absorb fat-soluble vitamins and form components of cell membranes
options.C: Dietary fats are only stored in the body
options.D: Dietary fats are only found in plant foods

questions.explanation: Dietary fats provide concentrated energy, supply essential fatty acids, help absorb fat-soluble vitamins and form components of cell membranes.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of fat?

options.A: Approximately 9 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of fat is approximately 9 kilocalories per gram.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are saturated and unsaturated fats?

options.A: Saturated fats have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty-acid chains; unsaturated fats have one or more double bonds
options.B: Saturated fats have double bonds; unsaturated fats have no double bonds
options.D: Saturated fats are always liquid at room temperature

questions.explanation: Saturated fats have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty-acid chains; unsaturated fats have one or more double bonds. Replacing some saturated fats with unsaturated fats is generally recommended for cardiovascular health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are trans fats?

options.A: Unsaturated fats containing at least one trans double bond; industrial trans fats increase cardiovascular risk and should be minimised or eliminated from the diet
options.B: Saturated fats with no double bonds

questions.explanation: Trans fats are unsaturated fats containing at least one trans double bond; industrial trans fats increase cardiovascular risk and should be minimised or eliminated from the diet.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is dietary fibre?

options.A: The parts of plant foods that are not fully digested in the small intestine; fibre supports bowel health and can help regulate blood glucose and blood cholesterol

questions.explanation: Dietary fibre refers to the parts of plant foods that are not fully digested in the small intestine; fibre supports bowel health and can help regulate blood glucose and blood cholesterol.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are vitamins?

options.A: Organic micronutrients needed in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth, immunity and body functions

questions.explanation: Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth, immunity and body functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?

options.A: Vitamins A, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which vitamins are water-soluble?

options.A: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins
options.B: Vitamins A, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins are water-soluble.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin A?

options.A: It supports vision, epithelial integrity, growth and immune function
options.D: It acts as an antioxidant only

questions.explanation: Vitamin A supports vision, epithelial integrity, growth and immune function.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can vitamin A deficiency cause?

options.A: Night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage that can lead to blindness

questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage that can lead to blindness.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin D?

options.A: It supports calcium and phosphorus absorption and normal bone mineralisation
options.D: It acts as an antioxidant only

questions.explanation: Vitamin D supports calcium and phosphorus absorption and normal bone mineralisation.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can vitamin D deficiency cause?

options.A: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; severe or prolonged deficiency can impair bone health

questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; severe or prolonged deficiency can impair bone health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin E?

options.A: It acts as an antioxidant and helps protect cell membranes

questions.explanation: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant and helps protect cell membranes.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin K?

options.A: It is required for normal blood clotting and also contributes to bone metabolism

questions.explanation: Vitamin K is required for normal blood clotting and also contributes to bone metabolism.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin C?

options.A: It supports collagen formation, wound healing, antioxidant defence and absorption of non-haem iron

questions.explanation: Vitamin C supports collagen formation, wound healing, antioxidant defence and absorption of non-haem iron.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can vitamin C deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy, which may cause bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing and fatigue

questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy, which may cause bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing and fatigue.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the role of vitamin B1 (thiamine)?

options.A: It supports carbohydrate metabolism and normal nerve function; deficiency can cause beriberi and Wernicke-related disorders

questions.question: What allows UHT products to have extended shelf life when unopened?

questions.subject: Food Science
questions.question: What does canning destroy in food?

questions.question: What do microorganisms convert during fermentation?

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What do food preservatives do?

questions.question: Which of the following are basic rules of food hygiene?

options.A: Keep clean; separate raw and cooked foods; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials

questions.explanation: The basic rules of food hygiene are: keep clean; separate raw and cooked foods; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: In the food danger zone, what happens to many foodborne bacteria?

options.A: They can multiply rapidly

questions.explanation: A commonly used food-safety teaching range is approximately 5°C to 60°C, in which many foodborne bacteria can multiply rapidly.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: When should handwashing be done in food handling?

options.A: After using the toilet, handling raw foods or touching waste

questions.explanation: Proper handwashing reduces transfer of pathogens from hands to food, utensils and surfaces, especially after using the toilet, handling raw foods or touching waste.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What causes foodborne diseases?

options.A: Consuming food or water contaminated with pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, chemicals or parasites

questions.explanation: Foodborne diseases are illnesses caused by consuming food or water contaminated with pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, chemicals or parasites.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What causes botulism?

options.A: Botulinum neurotoxin, commonly associated with improperly processed or stored foods

questions.explanation: Botulism is a potentially life-threatening illness caused by botulinum neurotoxin, commonly associated with improperly processed or stored foods; safe validated canning practices are essential.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Which moulds produce aflatoxins?

options.A: Certain Aspergillus moulds

questions.explanation: Aflatoxins are a group of toxic compounds produced by certain Aspergillus moulds, which can contaminate crops such as groundnuts and maize under favourable conditions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What does food testing assess?

options.A: Identity, composition, quality, contaminants, residues, additives, microbiological safety and compliance with standards

questions.explanation: Food testing is the analysis of food samples to assess identity, composition, quality, contaminants, residues, additives, microbiological safety and compliance with standards.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Which of the following information is provided on a food label?

options.A: Product identity, ingredients, allergens, nutrition information, net quantity, batch details, date marking, storage instructions and manufacturer or importer details

questions.explanation: A label provides prescribed information such as product identity, ingredients, allergens, nutrition information, net quantity, batch details, date marking, storage instructions and manufacturer or importer details.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: Under which Act was FSSAI established?

options.A: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006

questions.explanation: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India is the statutory authority established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What is FSSAI responsible for?

options.A: Laying down science-based food standards and regulating food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import to ensure safe and wholesome food

questions.explanation: FSSAI is responsible for laying down science-based food standards and regulating food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import to ensure safe and wholesome food.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What does HACCP identify and establish?

options.A: Food-safety hazards and controls at critical points in a process

questions.explanation: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points is a preventive system that identifies food-safety hazards and establishes controls at critical points in a process.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Safety
questions.question: What does food traceability track?

options.A: Food and its ingredients through stages of production, processing and distribution

questions.explanation: Food traceability is the ability to track food and its ingredients through stages of production, processing and distribution.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does nutrition involve?

options.A: The process by which the body obtains and uses food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, regulation and maintenance of health

questions.explanation: Nutrition is the process by which the body obtains and uses food substances for energy, growth, tissue repair, regulation and maintenance of health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which of the following are nutrients?

options.A: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water

questions.explanation: Nutrients are substances in food required by the body, including carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which nutrients are classified as macronutrients?

options.A: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats

questions.explanation: Macronutrients are nutrients required in relatively large amounts, principally carbohydrates, proteins and fats; water is also required in large amounts but does not provide energy.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which nutrients are classified as micronutrients?

options.A: Vitamins and minerals

questions.explanation: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals required in small amounts for normal growth, metabolism, immunity and other body functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does a balanced diet supply?

options.A: Adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts and proportions for a person's age, sex, activity, physiological state and health

questions.explanation: A balanced diet supplies adequate energy and all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts and proportions for a person's age, sex, activity, physiological state and health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of digestible carbohydrate?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of carbohydrates is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram for digestible carbohydrate, as a standard nutrition calculation factor.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are proteins made of?

options.A: Amino acids

questions.explanation: Proteins are molecules made of amino acids and are needed for growth, tissue repair, enzymes, hormones, transport proteins and immune functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of protein?

options.A: Approximately 4 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of protein is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Why must essential amino acids be obtained from the diet?

options.A: The human body cannot synthesise them in sufficient amounts
options.B: They are not needed by the body
options.C: They are found only in water

questions.explanation: Essential amino acids are amino acids that the human body cannot synthesise in sufficient amounts and therefore must obtain from the diet.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the energy value of fat?

options.A: Approximately 9 kilocalories per gram

questions.explanation: The energy value of fat is approximately 9 kilocalories per gram.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the structure of saturated fats?

options.A: They have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty-acid chains
options.B: They have one or more double bonds
options.C: They have at least one trans double bond

questions.explanation: Saturated fats have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty-acid chains; unsaturated fats have one or more double bonds.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the structure of unsaturated fats?

options.A: They have one or more double bonds in their fatty-acid chains
options.C: They have only trans double bonds

questions.explanation: Unsaturated fats have one or more double bonds in their fatty-acid chains.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the health concern with industrial trans fats?

options.A: They increase cardiovascular risk and should be minimised or eliminated from the diet

questions.explanation: Industrial trans fats increase cardiovascular risk and should be minimised or eliminated from the diet.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is dietary fibre?

options.A: The parts of plant foods that are not fully digested in the small intestine

questions.explanation: Dietary fibre refers to the parts of plant foods that are not fully digested in the small intestine; fibre supports bowel health and can help regulate blood glucose and blood cholesterol.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What health benefits does dietary fibre support?

options.A: Bowel health and regulation of blood glucose and blood cholesterol

questions.explanation: Fibre supports bowel health and can help regulate blood glucose and blood cholesterol.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are vitamins?

options.A: Organic micronutrients needed in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth, immunity and body functions

questions.explanation: Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small quantities for normal metabolism, growth, immunity and body functions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?

options.A: Vitamins A, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which vitamins are water-soluble?

options.A: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins
options.B: Vitamins A, D, E and K

questions.explanation: Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins are water-soluble.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What functions does vitamin A support?

options.A: Vision, epithelial integrity, growth and immune function

questions.explanation: Vitamin A supports vision, epithelial integrity, growth and immune function.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are the consequences of severe vitamin A deficiency?

options.A: Xerophthalmia and corneal damage that can lead to blindness

questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness and, in severe cases, xerophthalmia and corneal damage that can lead to blindness.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin D support?

options.A: Calcium and phosphorus absorption and normal bone mineralisation

questions.explanation: Vitamin D supports calcium and phosphorus absorption and normal bone mineralisation.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin D deficiency cause in children and adults?

options.A: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults

questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; severe or prolonged deficiency can impair bone health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the function of vitamin E?

options.A: It acts as an antioxidant and helps protect cell membranes

questions.explanation: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant and helps protect cell membranes.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is vitamin K required for?

options.A: Normal blood clotting and bone metabolism

questions.explanation: Vitamin K is required for normal blood clotting and also contributes to bone metabolism.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin C support?

options.A: Collagen formation, wound healing, antioxidant defence and absorption of non-haem iron

questions.explanation: Vitamin C supports collagen formation, wound healing, antioxidant defence and absorption of non-haem iron.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin C deficiency cause?

options.A: Scurvy, which may cause bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing and fatigue

questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy, which may cause bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing and fatigue.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin B1 (thiamine) support?

options.A: Carbohydrate metabolism and normal nerve function

questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) supports carbohydrate metabolism and normal nerve function; deficiency can cause beriberi and Wernicke-related disorders.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin B2 (riboflavin) form?

options.A: Coenzymes involved in energy metabolism

questions.explanation: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) forms coenzymes involved in energy metabolism; deficiency may cause inflammation of the mouth, lips and tongue.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does severe niacin deficiency cause?

options.A: Pellagra, classically associated with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia

questions.explanation: Vitamin B3 (niacin) forms NAD and NADP coenzymes; severe deficiency causes pellagra, classically associated with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is folate required for?

options.A: DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation

questions.explanation: Folate is required for DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation; adequate folate before and during early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does vitamin B12 deficiency cause?

options.A: Megaloblastic anaemia and neurological problems

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is required for DNA synthesis, red blood cell formation and normal nervous-system function; deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia and neurological problems.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is calcium essential for?

options.A: Bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signalling and blood clotting

questions.explanation: Calcium is essential for bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signalling and blood clotting.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is iron needed for?

options.A: Haemoglobin and oxygen transport and for several enzymes

questions.explanation: Iron is needed for haemoglobin and oxygen transport and for several enzymes.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is iodine needed to make?

options.A: Thyroid hormones, which regulate growth, development and metabolism

questions.explanation: Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones, which regulate growth, development and metabolism.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does zinc support?

options.A: Enzyme activity, growth, immunity, wound healing and normal taste and smell

questions.explanation: Zinc supports enzyme activity, growth, immunity, wound healing and normal taste and smell.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What do sodium and potassium help maintain?

options.A: Fluid balance, nerve impulses and muscle function

questions.explanation: Sodium and potassium help maintain fluid balance, nerve impulses and muscle function; excessive sodium intake can contribute to high blood pressure.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can excessive sodium intake contribute to?

options.A: High blood pressure

questions.explanation: Excessive sodium intake can contribute to high blood pressure.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does water support in the body?

options.A: Temperature regulation, transport of nutrients and waste, digestion, chemical reactions and maintenance of blood volume

questions.explanation: Water supports temperature regulation, transport of nutrients and waste, digestion, chemical reactions and maintenance of blood volume.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does malnutrition include?

options.A: Undernutrition, micronutrient-related malnutrition and overweight or obesity

questions.explanation: Malnutrition is a condition resulting from deficiencies, excesses or imbalances in energy and/or nutrients; it includes undernutrition, micronutrient-related malnutrition and overweight or obesity.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can undernutrition cause?

options.A: Wasting, stunting, underweight and micronutrient deficiencies

questions.explanation: Undernutrition is insufficient intake or utilisation of energy and nutrients, which can cause wasting, stunting, underweight and micronutrient deficiencies.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does wasting reflect?

options.A: Acute or recent undernutrition or illness

questions.explanation: Wasting is low weight for height or length, generally reflecting acute or recent undernutrition or illness.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does stunting reflect?

options.A: Chronic or long-term undernutrition and repeated illness

questions.explanation: Stunting is low height for age, generally reflecting chronic or long-term undernutrition and repeated illness.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does underweight in children reflect?

options.A: Low weight for age; it can reflect wasting, stunting or both

questions.explanation: Underweight in children is low weight for age; it can reflect wasting, stunting or both.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is overweight and obesity?

options.A: Excessive accumulation of body fat that may impair health
options.B: Insufficient intake of energy and nutrients

questions.explanation: Overweight and obesity refer to excessive accumulation of body fat that may impair health; assessment in adults commonly uses BMI alongside other clinical measures.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is BMI a screening measure for?

options.A: Body mass index is a screening measure, not a direct measurement of body fat or a complete diagnosis

questions.explanation: Body mass index is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared; it is a screening measure, not a direct measurement of body fat or a complete diagnosis.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does a balanced plate include?

options.A: A variety of cereals or millets, pulses or other protein foods, vegetables, fruits and appropriate amounts of milk/curd, nuts and oils

questions.explanation: A balanced plate is a practical meal-planning approach that includes a variety of cereals or millets, pulses or other protein foods, vegetables, fruits and appropriate amounts of milk/curd, nuts and oils, adapted to local foods and individual needs.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does dietary diversity improve?

options.A: The chance of meeting nutrient needs

questions.explanation: Dietary diversity is the consumption of a variety of food groups over a given period, improving the chance of meeting nutrient needs.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are examples of fortified foods?

options.A: Fortified salt or fortified edible staples

questions.explanation: Fortified foods are foods to which one or more micronutrients have been added in a controlled manner to improve nutritional quality, such as fortified salt or fortified edible staples.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the purpose of food fortification?

options.A: To improve nutritional quality and help prevent or correct deficiencies in a population
options.B: To reduce the price of food
options.C: To improve the colour of food
options.D: To increase the weight of food

questions.explanation: Food fortification is the deliberate addition of essential micronutrients to food to improve its nutritional quality and help prevent or correct deficiencies in a population.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: How is biofortification achieved?

options.A: Through plant breeding, agronomic practices or biotechnology

questions.explanation: Biofortification is increasing the nutrient content of crops through plant breeding, agronomic practices or biotechnology, for example iron- or zinc-rich crop varieties.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What causes anaemia?

options.A: Iron deficiency, other nutrient deficiencies, infections, genetic conditions and blood loss

questions.explanation: Anaemia is a condition in which haemoglobin concentration or red-cell mass is below the level needed for adequate oxygen transport; causes include iron deficiency, other nutrient deficiencies, infections, genetic conditions and blood loss.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What are common signs of anaemia?

options.A: Tiredness, weakness, pallor, breathlessness on exertion, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance

questions.explanation: Common signs of anaemia include tiredness, weakness, pallor, breathlessness on exertion, dizziness and reduced exercise tolerance, but diagnosis requires appropriate testing.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What causes iron-deficiency anaemia?

options.A: Insufficient iron for haemoglobin production, commonly associated with inadequate intake or absorption, blood loss, increased needs or parasitic/infectious conditions

questions.explanation: Iron-deficiency anaemia is anaemia caused by insufficient iron for haemoglobin production, commonly associated with inadequate intake or absorption, blood loss, increased needs or parasitic/infectious conditions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can improve non-haem iron absorption?

options.A: Vitamin C-rich foods with plant sources

questions.explanation: Vitamin C-rich foods with plant sources can improve non-haem iron absorption.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What can improve the availability of iron from phytate-containing foods?

options.A: Soaking, fermenting and dietary variety

questions.explanation: Phytates in some grains and legumes and polyphenols in tea or coffee can reduce absorption when consumed with meals; soaking, fermenting and dietary variety can help improve availability.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is IFA supplementation used for?

options.A: A public-health intervention used for specified population groups according to national programme protocols

questions.explanation: Iron and folic acid supplementation is a public-health intervention used for specified population groups according to national programme protocols; dose and schedule depend on age and physiological group.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does iodine deficiency during pregnancy and early life affect?

options.A: Brain development

questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency during pregnancy and early life can affect brain development.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the main population strategy for preventing iodine deficiency?

options.A: Universal salt iodisation

questions.explanation: Universal salt iodisation is the main population strategy; use adequately iodised salt while also limiting total salt intake.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is goitre?

options.A: Enlargement of the thyroid gland

questions.explanation: Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland; iodine deficiency is one cause, but goitre can also result from other thyroid conditions.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does child nutrition support?

options.A: Growth, brain development, immunity and lifelong health

questions.explanation: Child nutrition refers to nutrition during infancy and childhood that supports growth, brain development, immunity and lifelong health.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: For how long is exclusive breastfeeding recommended?

options.A: The first six months

questions.explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What type of complementary foods are recommended?

options.A: Age-appropriate, thick, nutrient-dense and diverse foods, prepared hygienically and fed responsibly

questions.explanation: Good complementary foods are age-appropriate, thick, nutrient-dense and diverse foods, including cereals or millets, pulses, vegetables, fruits and suitable animal-source foods where used, prepared hygienically and fed responsibly.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does the first 1,000 days concept consider a critical window for?

options.A: Maternal nutrition, fetal growth, infant feeding, brain development and prevention of growth faltering

questions.explanation: The first 1,000 days concept refers to the period from conception to a child's second birthday, considered a critical window for maternal nutrition, fetal growth, infant feeding, brain development and prevention of growth faltering.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does maternal nutrition support?

options.A: Maternal health, fetal growth, birth outcomes and lactation

questions.explanation: Maternal nutrition refers to adequate nutrition before, during and after pregnancy to support maternal health, fetal growth, birth outcomes and lactation.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What does adequate folic acid around conception and early pregnancy reduce the risk of?

options.A: Neural tube defects

questions.explanation: Adequate folic acid around conception and early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects; supplementation should follow national and clinical guidance.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Why is iron important during pregnancy?

options.A: It supports the increased blood volume and fetal development

questions.explanation: Pregnancy increases nutrient needs; iron supports the increased blood volume and fetal development, while folate supports cell division and neural tube development.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Why is folate important during pregnancy?

options.A: It supports cell division and neural tube development

questions.explanation: Folate supports cell division and neural tube development during pregnancy.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: What is the definition of low birth weight?

options.A: Birth weight below 2,500 grams, irrespective of gestational age

questions.explanation: Low birth weight is birth weight below 2,500 grams, irrespective of gestational age.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Security
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: What does food security require?

options.A: Physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets dietary needs and preferences for an active and healthy life

questions.explanation: Food security is a situation in which all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets dietary needs and preferences for an active and healthy life.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Security
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: Which of the following are the four dimensions of food security?

options.A: Availability, access, utilisation and stability

questions.explanation: The four dimensions of food security are availability, access, utilisation and stability.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Food Security
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: What does nutrition security include beyond food access?

options.A: Health, care, sanitation and other conditions needed for people to achieve good nutritional status

questions.explanation: Nutrition security refers to reliable access to adequate, safe and nutritious food together with health, care, sanitation and other conditions needed for people to achieve good nutritional status.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Public Health Nutrition
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: What does public health nutrition aim to reduce?

options.A: Nutrition inequalities

questions.explanation: Public health nutrition uses population-level policies and programmes to improve diets, prevent nutrient deficiencies and diet-related disease, and reduce nutrition inequalities.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Public Health Nutrition
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: What do dietary guidelines promote?

options.A: Health and disease prevention

questions.explanation: Dietary guidelines are evidence-based recommendations on food choices, dietary patterns and lifestyle practices intended to promote health and prevent disease; national guidance is periodically updated.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.chapter: Food Security and Public Health Nutrition
questions.question: What should be avoided when interpreting nutrient requirements?

options.A: Treating one number as suitable for everyone

questions.explanation: Requirements differ by age, sex and physiological condition, and scientific recommendations may be revised; avoid treating one number as suitable for everyone.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: What was the purpose of ICDS?

options.A: To provide an integrated package of nutrition, health and early-childhood services through Anganwadi Centres

questions.explanation: Integrated Child Development Services was launched on 2 October 1975 to provide an integrated package of nutrition, health and early-childhood services through Anganwadi Centres.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: What is the current umbrella framework for Anganwadi Services?

options.A: Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0

questions.explanation: Anganwadi Services, earlier known as ICDS, have been reorganised under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: What does Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 include?

options.A: Anganwadi Services, POSHAN Abhiyaan and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls
options.D: Only the Scheme for Adolescent Girls

questions.explanation: Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 includes Anganwadi Services, POSHAN Abhiyaan and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls, with a focus on nutrition outcomes and Anganwadi infrastructure.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: Who are the main beneficiaries of Anganwadi Services under POSHAN 2.0?

options.A: Children below six years, pregnant women and lactating mothers

questions.explanation: The main beneficiaries of Anganwadi Services under POSHAN 2.0 are children below six years, pregnant women and lactating mothers.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: What are the six services delivered through Anganwadi Services?

options.A: Supplementary nutrition; pre-school non-formal education; nutrition and health education; immunisation; health check-up; and referral services
options.C: Only pre-school education and health check-up
options.D: Only nutrition education and referral services

questions.explanation: The six services delivered through Anganwadi Services are supplementary nutrition; pre-school non-formal education; nutrition and health education; immunisation; health check-up; and referral services.
questions.source: Food Science and Nutrition Study Material

questions.subject: Government Programmes
questions.question: Which Anganwadi services are delivered through health-system infrastructure?

options.A: Immunisation, health check-ups and referral services
options.D: All six services are delivered only by Anganwadi workers

questions.explanation: Immunisation, health check-ups and referral services are delivered through the National Health Mission and public-health infrastructure, with Anganwadi platforms supporting coordination.
